title: Der Nagel
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 184. Text from Wikisource („Der Nagel (1857)“, twice proofread against the original). Fresh translation made directly from the German; 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: A merchant in too much of a hurry to have a loose horseshoe nail fixed loses first the shoe, then the horse, then arrives home late and ruined — a chain of small neglects each causing the next. The tale is barely a page, closer to a proverb acted out than a story, and it ends by naming its own moral: “Eile mit Weile,” more haste, less speed.

sentences.t: Ein Kaufmann hatte auf der Messe gute Geschäfte gemacht, alle Waaren verkauft und seine Geldkatze mit Gold und Silber gespickt.
sentences.l: A merchant had at the fair done good business, sold all wares and stuffed his money-belt with gold and silver.
sentences.i: A merchant had done good business at the fair: he had sold all his wares, and his money-belt was packed tight with gold and silver.
sentences.n: “Geschäfte machen” is to do business, and the plural Geschäfte is the everyday word for deals and dealings. gespickt comes from spicken, to lard a joint of meat with strips of bacon — the belt is larded, packed tight, with coin. Waaren is the 1857 spelling of Waren, goods; it has nothing to do with wahren, to keep safe.

sentences.t: Er wollte jetzt heimreisen und vor Einbruch der Nacht zu Haus sein.
sentences.l: He wanted now to travel home and before the falling-in of night to be at home.
sentences.i: He meant to travel home now and to be indoors before nightfall.
sentences.n: der Einbruch is from einbrechen, to break in: “Einbruch der Nacht” is nightfall, the moment the dark breaks in. zu Haus, without the -e, is the older form of zu Hause.

sentences.t: Er packte also den Mantelsack mit dem Geld auf sein Pferd und ritt fort.
sentences.l: He packed then the travelling-bag with the money onto his horse and rode off.
sentences.i: So he strapped the bag with the money onto his horse and rode off.
sentences.n: also is thus, so — never English “also.” der Mantelsack is the roll of baggage strapped on behind a rider. fortreiten is a separable verb and its particle fort waits at the end of the clause.

sentences.t: Zu Mittag rastete er in einer Stadt: als er weiter wollte, führte ihm der Hausknecht das Roß vor, sprach aber „Herr, am linken Hinterfuß fehlt im Hufeisen ein Nagel.“
sentences.l: At midday he rested in a town: when he wanted [to go] on, the house-servant led the steed out before him, but said “Sir, on the left hind foot a nail is missing in the horseshoe.”
sentences.i: At midday he halted in a town; when he was ready to go on, the ostler brought the horse out to him, but said, “Sir, there is a nail missing from the shoe on the left hind foot.”
sentences.n: “weiter wollte” has no verb of motion at all — wanted onward; German leaves it out after wollen, and the English supplies it in square brackets. vorführen is to lead an animal out and show it, with vor at the end. fehlen puts the missing thing in the nominative: ein Nagel fehlt, a nail is lacking. das Roß (modern Ross) is the higher word for a horse.

sentences.t: „Laß ihn fehlen,“ erwiederte der Kaufmann, „die sechs Stunden, die ich noch zu machen habe, wird das Eisen wohl fest halten. Ich habe Eile.“
sentences.l: “Let it be missing,” replied the merchant, “the six hours that I still have to make, the iron will surely hold fast. I have haste.”
sentences.i: “Let it be missing,” replied the merchant. “The shoe will hold well enough for the six hours I still have to cover. I am in a hurry.”
sentences.n: “laß ihn fehlen” — let it be lacking — is his whole answer to the warning. “Stunden machen” is to cover hours of road. wohl is not well here but a shrug of confidence: it will hold, no doubt. erwiederte is the 1857 spelling of erwiderte. “Ich habe Eile” is how German says I am in a hurry, and it will come back word for word.

sentences.t: Nachmittags als er wieder abgestiegen war und dem Roß Brot geben ließ, kam der Knecht in die Stube, und sagte „Herr, euerm Pferd fehlt am linken Hinterfuß ein Hufeisen. Soll ichs zum Schmied führen?“
sentences.l: In the afternoon, when he had got down again and had bread given to the steed, the servant came into the parlour, and said “Sir, your horse is missing a horseshoe on the left hind foot. Shall I lead it to the smith?”
sentences.i: In the afternoon, when he had dismounted again and had bread brought for the horse, the servant came into the room and said, “Sir, your horse has lost a shoe from the left hind foot. Shall I take it to the smith?”
sentences.n: “geben ließ” — lassen turns any verb into to have it done: he had bread given. euerm is the 1857 form of eurem; the servant addresses the merchant with the plural ihr, the polite form an inferior used. ichs is ich es run together.

sentences.t: „Laß es fehlen,“ erwiederte der Herr, „die paar Stunden, die noch übrig sind, wird das Pferd wohl aushalten. Ich habe Eile.“
sentences.l: “Let it be missing,” replied the gentleman, “the few hours that are still left over, the horse will surely hold out. I have haste.”
sentences.i: “Let it be missing,” replied the gentleman. “The horse will hold out well enough for the few hours that are left. I am in a hurry.”
sentences.n: The refusal comes a second time in nearly the same words; only the loss has grown, from the nail to the shoe. aushalten is to hold out, endure, with aus standing at the end of the clause.

sentences.t: Er ritt fort, aber nicht lange, so fieng das Pferd zu hinken an.
sentences.l: He rode off, but not long, so began the horse to limp.
sentences.i: He rode off, but not for long: the horse began to limp.
sentences.n: “nicht lange, so …” is a set narrative turn — not long, and then. anfangen is separable, and its an waits past the infinitive to the very end: fieng … an. fieng is the 1857 spelling of fing.

sentences.t: Es hinkte nicht lange, so fieng es an zu stolpern, und es stolperte nicht lange, so fiel es nieder und brach ein Bein.
sentences.l: It limped not long, so began it to stumble, and it stumbled not long, so fell it down and broke a leg.
sentences.i: It did not limp long before it began to stumble, and it did not stumble long before it went down and broke a leg.
sentences.n: The same turn three times over, each step worse than the one before: this chain is the tale. The horse is es because das Pferd is neuter, so German’s “it” here is a particular horse. niederfallen again leaves its particle at the end.

sentences.t: Der Kaufmann mußte das Pferd liegen lassen, den Mantelsack abschnallen, auf die Schulter nehmen und zu Fuß nach Haus gehen, wo er erst spät in der Nacht anlangte.
sentences.l: The merchant had to let the horse lie, unbuckle the travelling-bag, take [it] on the shoulder and go on foot home, where he arrived only late in the night.
sentences.i: The merchant had to leave the horse lying where it was, unbuckle the bag, take it on his shoulder and go home on foot, where he arrived only late in the night.
sentences.n: Four infinitives hang on the one mußte, and German is content to say the auxiliary once. “liegen lassen” is to leave lying. The object of nehmen is simply left out, since it is still the bag; the English supplies [it]. erst is not first here but not until, only.

sentences.t: „An allem Unglück,“ sprach er zu sich selbst, „ist der verwünschte Nagel Schuld.“
sentences.l: “For all the misfortune,” said he to himself, “is the cursed nail to blame.”
sentences.i: “The cursed nail is to blame for the whole misfortune,” he said to himself.
sentences.n: “an etwas Schuld sein” is to be to blame for something. The an-phrase is placed first for its weight, and since the verb must stand second in a German statement, ist arrives before its own subject. verwünscht is cursed, from verwünschen, to wish harm on.

The proverb the tale closes on: Eile mit Weile, haste with leisure — be quick, but give yourself the time. The rhyme Eile/Weile is what fixes it in the memory, and no English form keeps both the rhyme and the sense.

glossary.es: es — it (neuter pronoun; here the horse, das Pferd being neuter)
glossary.euerm: euer — your (dat. sg.; 1857 form of eurem, with the plural address ihr)
glossary.fest: fest — firm, tight, fast (adj./adv.; fest halten, festbinden, with fest standing at the end of the clause)
glossary.hufeisen: das Hufeisen — horseshoe (Huf, hoof + Eisen, iron; same form in the plural)
glossary.nagel: der Nagel — nail (here the nail that holds a horseshoe on)
glossary.roß: das Roß — steed, horse (1857 spelling of Ross; the higher, more formal word for a horse)
glossary.verkauft: verkaufen — sold (past part.; alle Waaren verkauft, sold all his wares)
glossary.waaren: die Waare — wares, goods (pl.; 1857 spelling of Waren)
